title: Two witnesses (Revelation 11)
hook: two prophets killed and raised; the kingdoms become the kingdom of our Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, the little scroll: honey in John's mouth, bitter once he'd swallowed it. Your line was sweet and bitter. What true thing tasted both ways for you? Day one thousand three hundred three.

Two bodies lie in the street of a great city. Nobody is allowed to bury them. People come from every nation to stare, and the mood is a party: neighbors trade gifts, glad that these two are finally quiet. The two had been prophets, dressed in sackcloth, saying things the city didn't want to hear. Now they're dead, and the street celebrates. Then, after three and a half days, something moves. Breath comes back into them. They stand up on their feet, and the people watching are terrified. A voice calls from heaven: come up here. And the two witnesses rise into a cloud while their enemies watch.

Revelation eleven names them plainly: "my two witnesses." A witness is someone who says what they've seen, out loud, even when it costs them. First, who are they? The text gives clues. They can shut the sky so no rain falls, and turn water into blood. Some readers hear Elijah, who shut the rain, and Moses, who turned the Nile to blood. Others read the two as a picture of the whole witnessing church. The text calls them "the two olive trees, and the two candlesticks standing before the God of the earth," and leaves it there. Second, where they die. Their bodies lie in the great city, the text says, "where also our Lord was crucified." Their story walks the road his walked: faithful words, a violent death, a watching crowd, and then, "the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet." Third, the trumpet. Soon after they rise, the seventh angel sounds, and loud voices in heaven say: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever." If that sounds familiar, Handel set very nearly those words in the Hallelujah chorus of his Messiah. Fourth, the street thought the story was over. The witnesses didn't win the argument by shouting louder. They kept saying what they'd seen. Three and a half days later, the text says, "great fear fell upon them which saw them," and the party went quiet.

Here's the practice: witness quietly today. Settle, and breathe. A witness isn't loud; a witness is honest about what they've seen. Think of one good thing you've seen with your own eyes. Kindness from a stranger. Someone who forgave. A prayer that held you up, if you pray. Hold it clearly, the faces, the place. Then ask: who might need to hear about it, simply, without a sermon? If you pray, you can ask for the chance and the courage. If you don't, just pick the person. The bell holds the time.
Two witnesses. The prophets of Revelation eleven who speak, are killed, lie in the street, and stand up again when the Spirit of life enters them.
Your line: he shall reign. Today, tell one person about one good thing you've actually seen. Keep it short, keep it true, and let it stand on its own. Day one thousand three hundred three.

howItsDone: Christians speak of bearing witness as telling, plainly and honestly, what they have seen of God, and choirs in churches and concert halls sing Revelation 11:15 in Handel's Hallelujah chorus.

fork.setup: you're in the great city. the two prophets who troubled everyone lie dead in the street. what does the crowd do?
options: leave them unburied, celebrate, and trade gifts.
go home quietly and say nothing.
fork.reveal: the crowd refuses them a grave and throws a party. then breath comes back into them, they stand up, and the watchers are afraid.

original.note: Greek: a witness, someone who testifies to what they have seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: two mysterious figures in an end-times puzzle.
what it means: two faithful speakers, killed and mocked, who rise when the Spirit of life enters them.
what a scholar hears: shut skies and water turned to blood, the signs of Elijah and Moses; and a death in the city where their Lord was crucified.

notes: 'Three and a half days' is from Revelation 11:9, 11 (three days and an half); kept because the cited text says it directly.
Identity of the witnesses: Moses and Elijah, or the witnessing church, given as 'some readers' / 'others'. Some early writers proposed Enoch and Elijah; omitted. Confirm.
Handel's Hallelujah chorus sets Revelation 11:15 in the singular ('The kingdom of this world is become...'); hence 'very nearly those words'. Confirm the claim is acceptable.
Original μάρτυς glossed only as 'a witness'; no etymology to 'martyr' given by design.

Editor pass: 'right after they rise' changed to 'soon after' (11:13 intervenes); stock 'why it matters on an ordinary day' cut; myth wording 'in the street' changed to 'onlookers' (11:9–10 says those dwelling on the earth).
Audit 2026-10-02: stock 'the last word wasn't the party' ending replaced with Revelation 11:11 ('great fear fell upon them which saw them'), added to sources.
